extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and students of astronomy / history of astronomy
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating solar and planetoid origin hypotheses
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing competing hypotheses for the origin of the planetoids and the constitution of the Sun (Laplace's nebular-ring hypothesis vs Olbers/exploded-planet hypothesis and models of the solar interior) using observational and inferential criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with planetoid mean-distance distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid origin hypothesis must account for the observed clustering of planetoids in a region between 2.50 and 2.80 (in terms of Earth's mean distance) with a peak near 2.65, and explain the contrast between this clustering and the wide scattering of a relatively few bodies at mean distances near 2 or exceeding 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exploded-planet hypothesis predicts a focal concentration near the original orbit (as observed); Laplace's broad nebulous ring must explain why it would concentrate so strongly at this distance. Use counts and mean distances (e.g., averages for early vs later discoveries) as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size-frequency distribution of planetoids
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis must explain why the number of small planetoids greatly exceeds the number of large ones, as evidenced by apparent magnitudes (e.g., only one exceeds 7th magnitude, many dozens are fainter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploded-planet models naturally produce many more smaller fragments; Laplace's model must account for this observed steep increase in small members with successive discoveries and telescope limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between fragment size and orbital deviation
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory theory should explain that the smallest fragments tend to show the widest deviations in mean distance and often the largest eccentricities and inclinations (examples: Vesta/Ceres vs Menippe/Eva; Hilda, Thule, Medusa among small/erratic ones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploded-planet expectations: large fragments fewer and nearer original orbit; smaller fragments propelled further and scattered more. Compare measured eccentricities and mean distances across size/magnitude groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity (or lack) of angular velocities in a nebulous ring
rubrics_metrics.description: The nebular hypothesis tacitly assumes similar angular velocities across parts of a nebulous ring; any viable model must reconcile this with observed disparities (e.g., periods of Thule 8.8 years vs Medusa 3.1 years imply large internal angular-velocity differences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate whether differential angular velocities implied by observed object periods are consistent with formation from a coherent ring; large implied differences weaken the Laplacian ring account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of wide range of eccentricities and inclinations
rubrics_metrics.description: A credible origin hypothesis must account for the great diversity of orbital eccentricities and inclinations among planetoids — both relative to neighbouring planets (Jupiter, Mars) and among the planetoids themselves (some differing by factors of many tens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the process invoked (uniform ring condensation vs explosive fragmentation) can plausibly produce the observed miscellaneously jumbled orbits and preserve individuality during separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-separation coexistence and survival of diverse motions
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis must explain how widely differing eccentricities and inclinations could have co-existed in the nebulous matter before separation and how such differences could survive the concentration and separation into discrete planetoids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider dynamical interactions during concentration: uniform-distribution assumptions vs fragment ejection scenarios; the inability to imagine plausible mechanisms counts against a hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entanglement vs concentricity of orbital 'rings' (D'Arrest observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed orbits, when represented as material rings, appear so entangled that one could lift one and lift the rest — a fact incompatible with Laplace's approximate concentric rings but congruous with an exploded-planet origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use orbital diagrams/representations to test whether the expected concentricity of a ring-formation model holds; entanglement favors explosive fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with meteors and shooting-star properties
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct hypothesis must harmonize with the natures and distributions of meteors and shooting stars; the mineral characters and required ejection velocities argue strongly against solar or volcanic planetary origins but fit derivation from planetary crust fragments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine meteor mineralogy (presence of iron, variety of kinds) and dynamics (needed velocities); volcanic or solar-jet origins are judged untenable due to mineral composition and inadequate ejection forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected production of a continuum of fragment sizes and streams
rubrics_metrics.description: The formation model should produce a wide spectrum from large planetoids (hundreds of miles) down to aerolites and innumerable smaller drops, and yield streams (meteor streams, solitary shooting stars) consistent with observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploded-planet mechanics (fissures, jets, condensation of metals/gases) offer a mechanism for producing masses across many size-scales and for creating elongated orbit-assemblages and meteor streams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association of short-period comets with the planetoid zone
rubrics_metrics.description: A viable account must explain why most short-period comets have orbits between Mars and Jupiter, periods similar to planetoids (3.1–8.8 years), and direct motions — suggesting kinship and possibly common origin with planetoids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the family of ~13 short-period comets (12 with aphelia within the planetoid zone) as evidence; an exploded-planet origin can account for cometary composition variability and associated meteoric swarms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections about the required age are not decisive
rubrics_metrics.description: The objection that an explosion must have occurred many millions of years ago is not a substantive disproof; either ancient or recent occurrence is equally reasonable and does not invalidate the explanatory power of the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject an otherwise explanatory model solely because it implies great antiquity; evaluate on match to phenomena rather than only timing plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrograde-motion objection and velocity calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis must account for the (non-)occurrence of retrograde motions among fragments: calculations (using Lagrange's estimated velocities) indicate fragments propelled backwards might not attain retrograde motion but develop highly elliptical direct orbits — a noted difficulty but potentially resolvable by undiscovered objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dynamical calculations to check whether explosion velocities would produce retrograde motions or merely reduce direct velocities to produce very elliptical orbits; lack of observed retrogrades is a challenge but not fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photosphere as an upper limit of an atmosphere of metallic gases
rubrics_metrics.description: A model of the Sun's constitution should treat the visible photosphere as the upper limit of an atmosphere of metallic vapours where condensation (precipitation) balances evaporation, producing luminous clouds that partly emit light and partly transmit light from the incandescent mass below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conception harmonizes with observed photospheric appearance and with Herschel's analogy to precipitate in a transparent fluid; evaluate models by whether they naturally produce such a photosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunspot explanation must reconcile emissivity and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Any model explaining sunspots as openings in the photosphere exposing non-luminous interior gases must address that if interior gases are non-luminous due to molecular dissociation, they should be transparent and thus would not appear dark when seen through openings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test spot-exposure hypotheses for internal consistency between emission and absorption/transmission properties; a physically consistent model should predict whether exposed interior regions appear darker or comparably bright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Molten-shell plus gaseous-nucleus model criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Sun consists of a molten metallic shell enclosing a hotter gaseous nucleus, the shell will be kept at the temperature where superficial parts vaporize, producing an atmosphere of metallic gases that condense into the photosphere; the model should also be congruous with the Sun's low specific gravity and photospheric phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether assumed internal structure (shell thickness, density, ongoing integration heat) yields the observed radiative properties and photospheric/cloud behavior; check for coherence with observed spot phenomena and spectral/photometric data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convective currents in a deep metallic-vapour atmosphere produce visible structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct solar-atmosphere model should predict ascending and descending currents whose tops and bases determine cloud thickness; tops of ascending currents will be regions of least condensed cloud and thus brightest, while adjacent thicker clouds produce contrasting appearances (relates to sunspot/network features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the expected scale of currents (dependent on atmospheric depth) to explain visible granular/spot-like features; compare to analogies (flocculent precipitates) and to observed photospheric structures.
